papers.title: High-Penetrance and Polygenic Germline Determinants of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: Insights From a Prospective Cohort
papers.authors: Rivera H, Morón-Duran F, García J, Marín R, Pérez-García J, Ramos-Muntada M
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The genetic basis of early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC) extends beyond established hereditary cancer syndromes, yet the contributions of rare high-penetrance variants, polygenic risk, and inherited immune-related genetic variation remain incompletely defined in prospectively recruited EOCRC patients. We evaluated monogenic and polygenic germline determinants of EOCRC as well as immune-related variants in an exploratory analysis, in a prospective cohort.
METHODS: We analyzed 101 prospectively recruited, consecutive EOCRC patients from the Spanish Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer Consortium (SECOC), an unselected multicenter cohort. Exome sequencing was used to identify pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in established hereditary cancer genes and candidate genes implicated in hereditary colorectal cancer (CRC)-related pathways. Polygenic risk was assessed in 72 genetically unresolved EOCRC patients using 203 established CRC risk alleles and compared with 1003 patients with CRC diagnosed at age ≥ 50 years and 1642 controls. An exploratory analysis of 47 immune-related CRC risk alleles was also performed.
RESULTS: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in established hereditary cancer genes were identified in 14% of EOCRC patients, predominantly affecting DNA mismatch repair genes. No convincing novel susceptibility genes were identified. Among genetically unresolved patients, approximately 15% had a polygenic risk above the 95th percentile of controls, a proportion comparable to that observed in patients with CRC diagnosed at age ≥ 50 years. In the exploratory immune-related analysis, no evidence of enrichment of immune-related risk alleles was observed in EOCRC.
CONCLUSIONS: EOCRC has a complex germline genetic architecture encompassing both established high-penetrance predisposition genes and polygenic susceptibility. Approximately one in seven patients carried a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in an established CRC predisposition gene, while a further subset of genetically unresolved patients had high polygenic risk, highlighting the substantial contribution of inherited genetic susceptibility to EOCRC.

papers.title: Validation of Newcastle ENDOPREM for assessing patient experience with colonoscopy: a multicenter prospective study
papers.authors: Liu B, Yang K, Shu H, Li X, Jiang Y, Luo S
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient experience is a key quality indicator for colonoscopy, yet standardized assessment tools are lacking in China. The Newcastle ENDOPREM scale has shown promise internationally but requires validation in China.
OBJECTIVE: To translate, adapt, and preliminarily evaluate the psychometric properties of the Chinese version of the Newcastle ENDOPREM (ENDOPREM-CN) to assess colonoscopy patient experience in Chinese patients.
METHOD: This dual-center prospective study followed forward-backward translation principles and cognitive interviewing for adaptation. From April 2024 to April 2026, 296 patients undergoing colonoscopy completed the ENDOPREM-CN. Reliability and validity were assessed, and factors influencing experience were analyzed.
RESULTS: Of 301 patients, 296 completed the ENDOPREM-CN. Positive experience was high (98.3%). Phase-specific findings showed 64.2% pre-procedure anxiety, 70.6% unpleasant bowel preparation taste, and, in terms of the post-procedure, 40.9% discomfort and 67.6% result concern. Total scale reliability was good (Cronbach's α = 0.86, KMO = 0.83); phase reliability ranged from excellent (before test, α = 0.93) to poor (bowel preparation, α = 0.41). Multivariate regression analysis identified factors including adequate information provision and anxiety about abnormal results (both P < 0.01) before the test, better-than-expected bowel preparation taste (P < 0.01), endoscopist gender preference (P = 0.05) and explanation about the procedure perceived right to terminate, embarrassment, discomfort frequency during the test (all P < 0.01), explanation of the results and clarity on next steps (both P < 0.01) after the test were associated with overall experience.
CONCLUSIONS: The ENDOPREM-CN shows acceptable overall reliability for measuring Chinese colonoscopy patients' experiences. Our findings underscore the importance of better patient communication, respecting patients' right to terminate procedures, and clear post-procedure results and follow-up to improve patient experience.

papers.title: When surgery unmasks the typhoid fever epidemic in Niger: a multicentre retrospective cohort study of 2,931 ileal perforations (2014-2019)
papers.authors: Bara A, Magagi M, Mahaman M, Maman B, Fils S, Bagnou H
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Typhoid fever remains a major public health challenge in low-income countries, where surgical complications particularly ileal perforation account for the greatest share of associated mortality. In Niger, restricted access to bacteriological investigations leads to substantial under recognition of the true disease burden.
OBJECTIVES: To describe the epidemiological, clinical, therapeutic, and outcome characteristics of presumed typhoid ileal perforations managed surgically in two referral hospitals in Niger, and to identify factors independently associated with in-hospital mortality.
METHODS: A multicentre retrospective descriptive study was conducted at the Zinder National Hospital (ZNH) and the Maradi Regional Hospital Centre (RHC/M) between January 2014 and December 2019. All patients who underwent surgery for acute peritonitis secondary to presumed typhoid ileal perforation, defined on the basis of epidemiological, clinical, and intraoperative criteria, were included. Factors associated with in-hospital mortality were identified by multivariate logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 2,931 cases of presumed typhoid ileal perforation were recorded among 4,271 operated acute peritonitis cases (68.6%). The mean age was 14.4 ± 11.2 years, with children and adolescents (1-15 years) representing 72.1% of cases. The male-to-female ratio was 1.8. Most patients came from rural areas (67.4%), and 71.3% were classified as indigent. The mean time from symptom onset to admission was 114.8 ± 62.2 h. Diverting ileostomy was the most frequently performed procedure (61.3%). Overall in-hospital case fatality was 11.2% (328/2,931). On multivariate analysis, rural origin (adjusted OR = 1.47; 95% CI: 1.13-1.86; p = 0.021) and indigent status (adjusted OR = 1.66; 95% CI: 1.21-2.07; p = 0.002) were independently associated with mortality.
CONCLUSION: Typhoid ileal perforations represent a substantial surgical burden in Niger, predominantly affecting children and socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Strengthening early diagnosis, expanding vaccine coverage notably through the recent introduction of the typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) into Niger's Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) and improving access to emergency surgical care are public health priorities.

papers.title: Expanding minimally invasive options in emergency general surgery: a multicentre evaluation of a novel MIS platform
papers.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
papers.authors: Cadière B, Mercoli H, Keller D
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Emergency general surgery (EGS) carries elevated morbidity, and minimally invasive surgery (MIS) may reduce surgical trauma but remains limited by staffing, logistical, and technical barriers. The Maestro® Platform is a collaborative robotic system designed to enhance surgeon autonomy during MIS. This study compares Maestro-assisted versus conventional laparoscopic EGS, stratified by procedure type.
METHODS: This multicentre retrospective study compared 24 Maestro-assisted EGS cases (July 2024-April 2025) with 25 consecutive conventional laparoscopic cases performed by the same surgical team. Outcomes analysed included surgery time, conversion rate, postoperative complications, length of stay, and 30-day mortality. Analysis was stratified by procedure type: appendectomy, emergency colectomy, and small bowel obstruction surgery. Additional Maestro cases without baseline comparators were reported descriptively.
RESULTS: Within comparable procedure groups, Maestro-assisted cases showed shorter surgery times: appendectomy (33.5 [31.5-42.3] vs. 76.0 [70.0-81.0] min, p = 0.002), emergency colectomy (135.0 [122.0-165.0] vs. 197.5 [159.3-220.0] min, p = 0.08), and small bowel obstruction (107.0 [28.0-110.0] vs. 108.0 [90.8-127.5] min, p = 0.54). No Maestro cases required conversion to open surgery, compared with 3 of 25 baseline cases (12%). Complication rates and length of stay were similar between groups. No device-related adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSION: In this preliminary procedure-stratified analysis, Maestro-assisted EGS was associated with shorter surgery times and a trend toward shorter length of stay and lower conversion rates in complex procedures such as colectomy, while maintaining comparable safety outcomes. The platform appeared adaptable across diverse emergency indications and may support minimally invasive approaches in emergency settings. Larger, prospective studies will be necessary to confirm these observations and define the role of collaborative robotic platforms in emergency surgical care.

papers.title: The oral-gut immune axis: a bidirectional hypothesis of the oral cavity as an immune programming hub for systemic and gut mucosal immunity
papers.authors: Wang Q, A L, Huan Y, Fang R, Cao C, Suo M
papers.abstract: The oral cavity has long been viewed simply as the site of food intake. Research in recent years has shown that the oral mucosa is a site of chronic low-grade inflammation that continuously produces inflammatory mediators. Given its specific structure, microbial products and immune mediators in the oral cavity can enter the bloodstream, while swallowed saliva continuously delivers oral microorganisms and their products to the gut. Oral dysbiosis, particularly in periodontitis, has been associated with systemic immune reprogramming, including trained immunity of monocytes, neutrophil priming, and expansion of gut-homing T helper 17 (Th17) cells. These modifications may contribute to intestinal barrier dysfunction, alterations in gut microbiota composition, and an increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. However, current evidence is largely associative: the presence of oral bacteria in intestinal tissue does not establish that they initiate intestinal disease, and an inflamed gut may itself favor the colonization of oral-derived taxa. Bidirectional influences between oral and gut inflammation therefore cannot be excluded, and reverse causation remains plausible. Genetic studies have identified polymorphisms in genes of innate immunity, such as nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2), interleukin-23 receptor (IL23R), and the interleukin-1 gene cluster (IL1 cluster), in both periodontitis and gastrointestinal diseases. However, because these loci are highly pleiotropic and have been associated with multiple inflammatory disorders affecting different organs, shared susceptibility genes alone cannot distinguish a genuine oral-to-gut axis from independent diseases sharing common immune-related genetic architecture. We propose the Oral-Gut Immune Axis (OGIA) here as a testable hypothesis, not as an established paradigm. OGIA is a predominantly, but not exclusively, oral-to-gut directional model that positions the oral cavity as a potential immune programming hub. Under specific genetic and microbial conditions, periodontal inflammation may act as an upstream contributor to gastrointestinal pathology. This framework generates testable predictions and identifies oral-targeted interventions as candidate preventive strategies, while acknowledging that current evidence remains insufficient to establish causality. Accordingly, the OGIA framework does not claim that microbial translocation is a demonstrated cause of human gastrointestinal disease. It treats translocation as one candidate mechanism among several, to be discriminated from systemic immune signaling in future studies.

papers.title: Application and future prospects of bispecific antibodies in the treatment of colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Long K, Zeng Y, Chen C, Yao Q
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, the incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) has continued to rise, imposing a substantial disease burden on both patients and society. Improvements in treatment strategies-including surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy-have significantly improved clinical outcomes. Immunotherapy, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors, has shown promising efficacy in rectal cancer studies. Nevertheless, multiple CRC subtypes are still hindered by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, the development of therapeutic resistance, and low response rates to immunotherapy, collectively limiting further gains in clinical benefit. As an emerging therapeutic modality, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) possess two binding specificities, enabling them to bind simultaneously to the same or different antigens, thereby generating multifaceted anti-tumor effects. Therefore, BsAbs can help overcome treatment resistance and potentiate antitumor immune responses. To date, numerous BsAbs have been used in clinical trials to assess their safety and efficacy across diverse CRC subtypes. This review summarizes the main classes of BsAbs used for CRC treatment, focusing on their mechanisms of action and recent advances in clinical research. We further discuss existing challenges for BsAbs and the potential strategies.

papers.title: Eosinophils in cancer immunity: context-dependent plasticity, biomarker potential, and therapeutic opportunities
papers.authors: Li N, Chen W, Zeng Y, Wang N, Wang J
papers.abstract: Eosinophils, traditionally associated with type 2 immunity, are increasingly recognized as context-dependent regulators of cancer immunity. Their effects are not intrinsically anti-tumorigenic or pro-tumorigenic but are shaped by five partially distinct dimensions of context: tumor type and stage, anatomical compartment and microlocalization, cytokine milieu and activation state, the circulating-versus-tissue compartment, and treatment exposure. This Review critically synthesizes mechanistic and clinical evidence defining this functional plasticity, with explicit separation of murine and human evidence throughout. Eosinophils can directly kill tumor cells through granule proteins and reactive oxygen species, recruit and activate cytotoxic lymphocytes, promote vascular normalization, and participate in interleukin-33-dependent anti-tumor circuits. In other settings, they can facilitate metastatic dissemination, angiogenesis, tissue remodeling, and immune suppression. These opposing functions help explain the heterogeneous clinical associations reported across malignancies. Tissue eosinophils at the invasive tumor front are associated with longer time to recurrence in colorectal cancer, whereas peripheral eosinophil dynamics have emerged as candidate biomarkers during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in non-small cell lung cancer; eosinophilic malignant pleural effusion may also define a distinct prognostic subgroup. We critically distinguish prognostic, predictive, and pharmacodynamic biomarker claims, and emphasize that most reported associations remain prognostic rather than demonstrated predictors of treatment benefit. We further discuss therapeutic opportunities involving the interleukin-5/interleukin-33/eotaxin axis, induced eosinophils, and eosinophil-assisted cellular therapy, graded by their level of clinical maturity and weighed against the risks of systemic eosinophil activation. We argue that clinically useful eosinophil biomarkers will require integration of abundance with phenotype, spatial localization, tissue compartment, and treatment context. This framework clarifies when eosinophils are protective, harmful, or therapeutically exploitable and highlights priorities for prospective human studies in cancer immunology and precision immunotherapy.

papers.title: Anatomical stratification and robot-assisted radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer after colorectal cancer surgery
papers.authors: Liu S, He Y, Gu Z
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) and prostate cancer (PCa) are the most common malignancies of the digestive and genitourinary tracts in men, respectively, and their coexistence is increasing as populations age and survival improves. Second primary PCa is the most frequent second primary malignancy among male CRC survivors, yet current guidelines provide no dedicated recommendations for diagnosis or treatment in this setting. Pelvic anatomy after CRC surgery is not uniform: the prior colorectal procedure determines the relationship between the colorectal anastomosis and the posterior aspect of the prostate, and therefore whether the Denonvilliers fascia-anterior rectal space is preserved, scarred or absent. This variable is the principal determinant of surgical difficulty and approach choice and can be assessed preoperatively. Drawing on a SEER analysis and published evidence, this review summarises the epidemiological association and shared mechanisms of the two tumours (host and metabolic factors, molecular pathways, genetic susceptibility and treatment-related second primaries), describes procedure-specific anatomical and functional changes, and proposes an approach-selection matrix defined by two independent axes: abdominal access difficulty and posterior-plane risk. Transperitoneal, extraperitoneal, single-port transvesical and transperineal routes are compared, followed by a seven-step surgical framework for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy, together with oncological and functional outcomes, complications and centre-level quality control. The reverse challenge of CRC developing after PCa treatment, and the limitations of a predominantly retrospective evidence base, are also discussed. The resulting anatomy-based framework links the pre-treatment colorectal history to a reproducible diagnostic and surgical strategy for PCa in CRC survivors.

papers.title: Jiedu Sangen Decoction for Colorectal Cancer: Pharmacological Mechanisms, Network Pharmacology Perspective and the Interaction With Gut Microbiota
papers.authors: Zhu Z, Guo S, Gao W, Liu Q, Shen M, Ruan S
papers.abstract: Jiedu Sangen Decoction (JSD) is a traditional Chinese medicine formula used in the management of colorectal cancer (CRC). This review critically summarizes current evidence on the pharmacological effects of JSD, integrating experimental studies of the complete formula, network pharmacology predictions, mechanistic evidence from its constituent herbs and compounds, and potential interactions with the gut microbiota. Experimental studies of the complete JSD formula indicate that it can inhibit CRC cell proliferation and promote apoptosis, suppress invasion and metastasis through regulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition(EMT) and cancer-associated fibroblasts(CAFs), and enhance sensitivity to 5-fluorouracil by modulating glycolytic metabolism. Network pharmacology further suggests a multi-component and multi-target mode of action involving candidate hub targets and signaling pathways that partially converge with experimentally observed mechanisms. Individual JSD-associated compounds also exhibit diverse anticancer and microbiota-modulating activities; however, these findings should be regarded as supportive mechanistic evidence rather than direct evidence for the complete formula. In particular, direct evidence that JSD modulates the gut microbiota or microbial metabolites in CRC remains limited. Moreover, despite accumulating preclinical findings, high-quality clinical evidence evaluating the efficacy and safety of JSD in CRC is currently insufficient. Further studies integrating standardized chemical characterization, mechanistic validation, microbiome research, and well-designed clinical investigations are needed to establish the translational relevance of JSD in CRC.

papers.title: Biological characteristics of secreted modular calcium-binding protein 2 and its mechanisms in disease progression: Current advances in targeted therapies
papers.authors: Lan T, Wang R, Liu F, Wang Q, Yan Q, Liu X
papers.abstract: Secreted modular calcium-binding protein 2 (SMOC2) is a secreted matricellular protein belonging to the SPARC family. It is widely distributed throughout the body and plays complex roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and pathological conditions such as fibrosis, cancer, and inflammation. By regulating multiple key signaling pathways, SMOC2 can exert pathogenic and protective effects on cellular behavior. Studies involving human samples, animal models, and cell experiments have shown that SMOC2 is implicated in fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transformation and may contribute to fibrosis in the heart, kidneys, lungs, and liver. However, in cancer, SMOC2 exhibits context-dependent duality: it exerts tumor-suppressive effects in gastric and hepatocellular carcinomas, whereas it has been reported to promote tumor progression in renal, gallbladder, pancreatic, and endometrial cancers. Additionally, its functional role in colorectal cancer appears spatially dichotomous-largely tumor-suppressive in the tumor bulk but pro-invasive at the invasive front in some models-and requires further elucidation. This narrative review examines the pathological roles of SMOC2, with particular attention to its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target, and discusses the challenges associated with its clinical translation.
